title: One Missed Separation, One Extra Chromosome

scenes.visual: Title card: One Missed Separation, One Extra Chromosome. Subtitle: Chromosome dose changes development.

scenes.tts: A cell with an extra or missing chromosome has the wrong dose of the genes on it. That can change development. Most aneuploid human embryos do not survive pregnancy. Trisomy twenty-one is one of the few autosomal trisomies seen regularly at birth. It means three copies of chromosome twenty-one instead of two, and causes Down syndrome. The important change is the extra dose of genes. How does a cell get that extra chromosome?
scenes.narration: A cell with an extra or missing chromosome has the wrong dose of the genes on it. That can change development. Most aneuploid human embryos do not survive pregnancy. Trisomy 21 is one of the few autosomal trisomies seen regularly at birth. It means three copies of chromosome 21 instead of two, and causes Down syndrome. The important change is the extra dose of genes. How does a cell get that extra chromosome?

scenes.visual: Open on two copies of chromosome 21, each with the same marked gene positions. Add a third chromosome and a third copy of every marked gene. Label the change “Extra chromosome → extra gene dose → altered development”. Show the text “Most aneuploid human embryos do not survive pregnancy”, then identify trisomy 21 as a survivable example associated with Down syndrome. End with the question about the extra chromosome; omit the historical laboratory sequence.

scenes.tts: Extra X chromosomes are better tolerated. Mammalian cells silence every X beyond one, so extra X chromosomes add little active dose. But some genes escape this silencing. Extra active copies of those genes are thought to explain many features of Klinefelter syndrome, usually an extra X in a male.

scenes.visual: Contrast the fully highlighted extra chromosome 21 with an extra X that becomes mostly dim. Leave escape-gene positions lit on both X chromosomes. Label the male XXY example “Klinefelter syndrome”; show “Most extra X genes silenced; some escape”. Avoid depicting complete X silencing or complete dosage compensation.

scenes.tts: Nondisjunction is a failure of chromosomes to part when a cell divides. At meiosis one, the two homologues of each pair separate. At meiosis two, the sister chromatids separate. Follow chromosome twenty-one in one human spermatocyte. Assume one error, otherwise normal divisions, and recovery of all four products.
scenes.narration: Nondisjunction is a failure of chromosomes to part when a cell divides. At meiosis I, the two homologues of each pair separate. At meiosis II, the sister chromatids separate. Follow chromosome 21 in one human spermatocyte. Assume one error, otherwise normal divisions, and recovery of all four products.
scenes.caption: Nondisjunction is a failure of chromosomes to part when a cell divides. At meiosis I, the two homologues of each pair separate. At meiosis II, the sister chromatids separate. Follow chromosome 21 in one human spermatocyte. Assume one error, otherwise normal divisions, and recovery of all four products.
scenes.visual: Show a normal two-division overview with blue and yellow homologues and paired sister chromatids. Label meiosis I as homologue separation and meiosis II as sister separation. Then focus on chromosome 21 in a spermatocyte. Display the model assumptions: one error, other divisions normal, all four products recovered.

scenes.tts: Suppose both homologues go to the same cell at meiosis one. Meiosis two then runs normally. That cell gives two sperm, each with two copies of chromosome twenty-one. These are disomic sperm. The other cell has no chromosome twenty-one. Its two sperm have none. These are nullisomic sperm.
scenes.narration: Suppose both homologues go to the same cell at meiosis I. Meiosis II then runs normally. That cell gives two sperm, each with two copies of chromosome 21. These are disomic sperm. The other cell has no chromosome 21. Its two sperm have none. These are nullisomic sperm.
scenes.caption: Suppose both homologues go to the same cell at meiosis I. Meiosis II then runs normally. That cell gives two sperm, each with two copies of chromosome 21. These are disomic sperm. The other cell has no chromosome 21. Its two sperm have none. These are nullisomic sperm.
scenes.visual: Retain the meiosis I failure diagram: both blue and yellow homologues enter one secondary cell. After normal meiosis II, show two sperm with one blue and one yellow chromosome each, and two sperm with no chromosome 21. Label the two groups disomic and nullisomic. Retie all phrase cues to the revised narration.

scenes.tts: Now meiosis one is normal, but sisters fail to part in one cell at meiosis two. This gives one disomic sperm and one with none. The other cell gives two normal sperm. Joined to a normal egg, a disomic sperm makes a zygote with three copies of chromosome twenty-one. A sperm with none makes a zygote with only one.
scenes.narration: Now meiosis I is normal, but sisters fail to part in one cell at meiosis II. This gives one disomic sperm and one with none. The other cell gives two normal sperm. Joined to a normal egg, a disomic sperm makes a zygote with three copies of chromosome 21. A sperm with none makes a zygote with only one.

scenes.visual: Retain the meiosis II error diagram, with normal homologue separation followed by failed sister separation in just one secondary cell. Show one disomic, one nullisomic and two normal sperm. Fertilize a normal egg with a disomic sperm to show trisomy, and separately with a nullisomic sperm to show monosomy. Keep the same blue/yellow homologue colors and grey egg chromosome.

scenes.tts: That is the model. In people, most free trisomy twenty-one comes from the mother, and most maternal errors arise at meiosis one. The risk rises with the mother's age. A missed separation changes chromosome number. The extra or missing genes change the dose, with consequences for development and survival.
scenes.narration: That is the model. In people, most free trisomy 21 comes from the mother, and most maternal errors arise at meiosis I. The risk rises with the mother's age. A missed separation changes chromosome number. The extra or missing genes change the dose, with consequences for development and survival.

scenes.visual: Replace both parental-marker exercises with one human-context scene. Label “Most free trisomy 21: maternal origin” and “Most maternal errors: meiosis I”. Show a qualitative upward arrow labelled “Risk rises with maternal age”, without numerical axes or invented rates. End on “Missed separation → extra or missing chromosome → altered gene dose → development and survival”. Do not imply that every error is maternal or that the classical model explains every human egg error.
End card holds the causal chain: Missed separation → changed chromosome dose → consequences for development and survival.
